youtube_description:
Twice, the Mongol Empire sent fleets against Japan. Before the second came, a young regent had beheaded the Khan's envoys and refused every demand. Hojo Tokimune ruled Kamakura from his teens, and his choices were courage, ruthlessness and isolation all at once. This is the story of what he did, what the wind did, and what it all cost him.

scenes.narration: In the thirteenth century, one power overshadowed every other on earth. The Mongols had swept across Asia and into Europe, and by the 1260s Kublai Khan stood at the head of the largest land empire in history. Korea had been forced to submit after decades of war, and its shipyards and sailors now served the Khan. Southern China was next. Only one neighbor remained across the water, a chain of islands whose rulers had never seen a Mongol soldier. Kublai decided that Japan could be asked to kneel, and he chose to ask politely, at first.

scenes.narration: Across that water lay Kamakura, seat of Japan's first warrior government. The shogun there was a figure of ceremony. Real power belonged to the Hojo family, who ruled as regents, called shikken, in the shogun's name. In 1251, a boy was born into that family: Tokimune, son of the formidable Hojo Tokiyori. He was raised from childhood to rule, schooled in Zen discipline and in the politics of a clan that survived by outmaneuvering its rivals. Nobody could have guessed how soon the weight of that world would fall on him.

scenes.narration: In 1268, a Korean envoy arrived at the Japanese outpost in Kyushu carrying a letter from Kublai Khan. Its tone was courteous, but its meaning was not. It spoke of friendship, then hinted that no ruler wished to settle matters by force. Within two months, Tokimune, still a teenager, was named regent of the Kamakura government. A boy who had so far served only as co-signer to his elders now held a letter that could mean war with the greatest army in the world. And he had to decide what to do.

scenes.narration: The imperial court in Kyoto leaned toward a formal, carefully worded reply. The thinking was simple: keep talking and avoid a war. But the court did not command the warriors, and Tokimune did. He ordered that no reply be sent. Over the following years, more envoys came, each carrying the same demand, and each was sent away empty-handed. Silence was a message of its own, and Tokimune knew that it might be answered with ships. He chose it anyway.

scenes.narration: He did not simply wait. In 1271, Tokimune ordered the warrior houses of Kyushu to guard the western coast against a foreign attack, and he tightened Hojo control over the region's defenses. Those who ignored the order faced punishment, in a government built on loyalty in exchange for land. Along the beaches near Hakata, men began to watch the horizon. Few believed the Mongols would truly cross the sea. Tokimune seems to have believed it completely.

scenes.narration: Danger also lived inside the Hojo house. In 1272, Tokimune ordered several relatives killed, among them his older half-brother, Hojo Tokisuke, whose position made him a rival. The affair is now called the Nigatsu Disturbance. It protected the government from division on the eve of war, but at a terrible price. Still in his early twenties, Tokimune ruled alone, among men who had every reason to fear him, and with no one he could completely trust.

scenes.narration: The Mongols came in November 1274. A combined Mongol and Korean fleet, hundreds of ships carrying tens of thousands of men, first struck the island of Tsushima, then Iki. The small garrisons fought and died almost to the last man. Island villages burned, and survivors were carried away. Messengers raced across the water to the mainland. Within days, warriors from all over Kyushu were riding toward Hakata Bay. Tokimune's long silence had been answered.

scenes.narration: At Hakata, the Japanese met an enemy who fought nothing like them. Later accounts say samurai rode out to announce their names and seek single combat. The invaders moved in dense formations to the beat of drums and gongs, firing volleys of arrows, some said poisoned, and hurling explosive projectiles whose thunderous noise terrified the horses. The defenders gave ground. By nightfall they had fallen back inland, and Hakata lay in enemy hands.

scenes.narration: Then, the next morning, the bay was empty. The invaders had vanished. Korean accounts record a storm that cost a number of ships during the retreat. Historians debate the rest: heavy losses, dwindling arrows, a reconnaissance that had achieved its aim, or simply a decision to leave before the weather turned. Whatever the cause, Kyushu was saved for the moment. In Kamakura, Tokimune did not celebrate. He seems to have assumed that the Mongols had only been testing the shore, and that they would return with more.

scenes.narration: In the spring of 1275, Kublai sent another group of envoys, led by a man named Du Shizhong. They landed in Nagato and were taken to Kamakura. Tokimune had a decision to make. Receiving them would signal weakness, and releasing them would change nothing. He ordered the party beheaded at Tatsunokuchi, the execution ground beside the sea. To the Mongols, who treated envoys as sacred, it was an unforgivable insult. It was also a message that Japan would not negotiate in the shadow of ships.

scenes.narration: Tokimune knew what the execution had bought him: a second invasion. So he used the time. In 1276 he ordered the warriors of Kyushu to build a stone wall along the shore of Hakata Bay, each province assigned its own stretch. In the following years it grew to some twenty kilometers, perhaps two to three meters high on the seaward side. He also gathered ships and sailors, and even planned an attack on Korea, an idea later dropped. Japan's answer to the greatest army on earth was masonry and planning.

scenes.narration: In 1279, the Southern Song fell, and Kublai's armies were free to look east. Another Mongol mission came to Hakata, and once more Tokimune ordered the envoys beheaded. There would be no negotiation, no tribute, and no turning back. That same year, the Chinese Zen master Mugaku Sogen arrived in Kamakura at Tokimune's invitation. The regent who had condemned so many to death found in Zen the discipline he needed: the ability to face fear without being ruled by it.

scenes.narration: In the summer of 1281, the Mongols came back with a force Japan had never imagined. By Yuan records, two fleets: roughly forty thousand men sailing from Korea and about a hundred thousand from southern China. The fleet from Korea reached Hakata first, in June. The shore was no longer open. The stone wall blocked their landing, and small Japanese boats slipped out at night to board and burn ships. For almost two months, the invaders stayed at sea or on narrow footholds, trapped by the defenses Tokimune had demanded.

scenes.narration: In mid-August, as the vast fleet crowded the waters off Takashima and Imari Bay, a great typhoon rose out of the night. Ships anchored close together, some perhaps hastily built river boats, were smashed against one another and against the rocks. Thousands drowned. Japanese records called it divine, and it would later be named kamikaze, the divine wind. Mongol commanders reportedly abandoned many of their men and sailed away with whatever ships still floated.

scenes.narration: Survivors stranded on Takashima and along the coast were hunted down by the Japanese warriors who had been waiting for this chance. Chinese sources admit that only a fraction of the force returned. Many of those left behind were killed or taken captive. Kublai did consider a third expedition, but it never sailed. For the second time, the Mongol Empire had failed to conquer Japan. But Tokimune, far away in Kamakura, would not get to claim a victory. He still had to pay for it.

scenes.narration: The war was over, but paying for it was a different battle. Warriors who had fought, and temples that had prayed for victory, expected land as a reward. A defensive war produces no conquered territory, and Tokimune had little to hand out. In 1282, he founded Engakuji in Kamakura, with Mugaku Sogen as its first abbot, to pray for the dead of both sides, Japanese and Mongol. The regent who had beheaded envoys now paid for the souls of his enemies.

scenes.narration: He stayed in command at Kamakura, and kept the coast guarded, preparing for a third assault. The strain wore him down. In April 1284, Hojo Tokimune died, at only thirty-two years old. On that same day, he shaved his head and took Buddhist vows. A later tradition says that when he once confessed his fear to Mugaku Sogen, the master told him to look for who it was that felt afraid. Whether or not that is true, he had spent his short life facing what no teenager should have to face.

scenes.narration: So did the divine wind save Japan? Not alone. Without the wall, the garrisons and years of preparation, the fleets of 1281 might have landed and fought on land, where their numbers counted. The typhoon destroyed an army that had already been pinned on the water. Tokimune's real strength was refusal: refusing to answer, refusing to submit, refusing to flinch. But it left the Hojo regime with unrewarded warriors and an empty treasury, strains that helped bring down the Kamakura shogunate in 1333, about fifty years later.

scenes.narration: Hojo Tokimune never saw the third invasion he feared, and he never lived to see what his decisions would cost. He chose confrontation at an age when most men are still choosing a career, and he paid for it with his short life. Courage, ruthlessness and luck all played a part, and history rarely tells us where one ends and another begins. If you want to keep exploring such questions, you know where to find us.
